solutions.check: grid and clues read from the FT's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; every fifteensquared answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: "Very large in glee" misconstrues Hamlet's plot

indicators.note: to misconstrue is to read wrongly, so the quoted words get rearranged into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone garbles a quotation, mistaking it for a summary of Hamlet's storyline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hamlet's plot' looks like the Shakespeare play's storyline; it is a small village's piece of land. 'misconstrues' rearranges V, LARGE, IN and GLEE.
explanation.definitionFit: A hamlet is a small settlement, and the plot of common grassland at its centre is the classic English shared space.

clue.text: Caligula's sex position many came to see

parts.note: sex is Latin for six, and Caligula as a Roman emperor would write six in Roman numerals as VI
a site is a position or location
D is the Roman numeral for 500, a crossword stand-in for many

explanation.surface: A racy reference to the Roman emperor's preferred bedroom position that drew crowds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sex' is not about bedrooms: it is the Latin word for six, written VI as a Roman would.
explanation.definitionFit: Visiting a place or person is going there in order to see them, so the past tenses match.

clue.text: Heroic lover with piercing eye

indicators.note: one piece piercing another means it sits inside it, so the word for with goes into the word for eye

parts.note: to eye someone suggestively is to leer at them
and means with, as in bread and butter

explanation.surface: A romantic hero with a penetrating gaze.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heroic' means belonging to Hero: in Greek myth Leander swam the Hellespont nightly to visit his beloved Hero.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Greek legend this young man was the lover of Hero, priestess of Aphrodite at Sestos.

clue.text: Leader on Annapurna gets ill — right to receive treatment and physician

indicators.note: the leader on a word is its opening letter, here of the Himalayan peak's name
letters receiving treatment are worked over and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A climber falls sick on a Himalayan peak and is entitled to medical care and a doctor.
explanation.walkthrough: Annapurna is a Himalayan mountain; its first letter A starts the answer. 'to receive treatment' rearranges GETS ILL with R.
explanation.definitionFit: An allergy specialist is a doctor who diagnoses and treats allergic conditions.

clue.text: Artistic support for treacherous person beheaded

indicators.note: a word beheaded loses its first letter, its head

parts.note: a weasel is a sly, untrustworthy person

explanation.surface: Funding an artist turns out to be backing a traitor who is then executed.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter's stand holds the canvas while the artist works, a literal support for art.

clue.text: Cheese on toast provides unusually good mouthful

parts.note: rare can mean exceptionally fine, as in a rare treat
a bit is a small morsel of food

explanation.surface: Cheese on toast makes for an exceptionally tasty snack.
explanation.definitionFit: Welsh rarebit is the traditional British dish of melted seasoned cheese grilled on toast.

clue.text: Sent into stormily sea-girt land

indicators.note: girt means surrounded, so one set of letters is wrapped round the other
stormily suggests wild disorder, so the letters of sea are scrambled
sent can mean sent into a frenzy or transported, so the letters of into are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is dispatched in a storm to a country surrounded by the sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent' looks like the surface's verb but is an anagram signal, and 'stormily' another; 'girt' (surrounded) wraps ESA round TONI.
explanation.definitionFit: This Baltic republic is a country, a land in the political sense.

clue.text: Rude Posh attends dance club, sure to get thrown out

indicators.note: attends here means comes along after, so the posh letter follows the club

parts.note: a disco is a nightclub for dancing
U is the label for upper-class usage, so it stands for posh

indicators.note: letters thrown out are tossed about and land in a new order

explanation.surface: A snooty celebrity at a nightclub behaves badly and is sure to be ejected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Posh' reads as a celebrity's nickname but is U, the old label for upper-class speech. 'get thrown out' rearranges SURE TO into RTEOUS.
explanation.definitionFit: Discourteous behaviour lacks politeness, which is what being impolite or uncivil means.

clue.text: Is to secure new, extravagant place

indicators.note: to secure something is to hold it fast inside, so the word for new goes within

parts.note: taken as written
tall can mean exaggerated or excessive, as in a tall story

explanation.surface: Someone is about to buy a brand-new, lavish home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'place' looks like a noun for a home, but it is a verb; TALL is extravagant as in 'a tall order'.
explanation.definitionFit: To install a fitting is to put it in position, a synonym of setting something in place.

clue.text: Star unfit with belly layer

indicators.note: an unfit star is out of shape, so the four letters are put into another form

parts.note: tum is an informal word for belly

explanation.surface: An out-of-condition celebrity with a paunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfit' rearranges STAR into STRA.
explanation.definitionFit: A stratum is one horizontal bed of rock or soil, or one level within a society.

clue.text: Reckon why men worked with tool

indicators.note: worked means kneaded or shaped, so the letters are reformed

explanation.surface: Someone wonders why the men laboured with a hand tool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'worked' rearranges RECKON WHY MEN.
explanation.definitionFit: An adjustable spanner of this kind is a hand implement for gripping nuts and pipes.

clue.text: Dodgy doctor stashing drugs in some department

indicators.note: stashing means hiding something away inside, so the drugs letter goes within
dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so the letters are bent out of order

parts.note: E stands for ecstasy, the drug

explanation.surface: A crooked doctor hides narcotics in some hospital department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'department' is not a hospital ward but one of France's administrative areas, named after the Burgundy hills. E is ecstasy.
explanation.definitionFit: Côte-d'Or is one of the administrative areas of France, in Burgundy, so it is one such department.

clue.text: Country person of vulgar habits heading off sometime soon

indicators.note: with its heading off a word loses its first letter

parts.note: pleb is a derogatory word for a common, uncouth person
anon is an old word for soon, before long

explanation.surface: A boorish person leaves the country before long.
explanation.definitionFit: Lebanon is a Middle Eastern nation on the eastern Mediterranean coast.

clue.text: Buried during ancient city's catastrophic end

indicators.note: the setter uses during to mean within, so the scrambled end sits inside the city

parts.note: Ur was an ancient Sumerian city in what is now southern Iraq

indicators.note: a catastrophic end is a wrecked one, so its letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Something was entombed when an ancient city met its disastrous downfall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'during' is used loosely to mean inside; Ur is the ancient Mesopotamian city famed in the Bible as Abraham's birthplace.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lying under the ground is interred or covered over, the same sense as being entombed.

clue.text: Nervous Shakespeare women dismissed with some banter

indicators.note: women dismissed means the letter for women is sent away from the name

parts.note: Will is the playwright William Shakespeare's first name
a means one, some single instance
to tease is to banter, so a tease is a bit of banter

explanation.surface: The Bard's heroines feel jittery after being sent off with some teasing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shakespeare women' looks like his heroines, but the women are just W, taken out of WILL.
explanation.definitionFit: Being uncomfortable and anxious is the common idiom's meaning, matching jittery or nervous.

clue.text: Parishioner's poem sung for each boy

parts.note: a lay is a short lyric poem meant to be sung
per means for each, as in a pound per head
a son is a male child

explanation.surface: A churchgoer's verse is sung for every lad.
explanation.definitionFit: A layperson is a non-clergy member of the church, the ordinary churchgoer of a parish.

clue.text: With sixth sense they leap in dance across time

indicators.note: the dancers move across the time letter, putting it inside their reordered letters
words in dance whirl about and come out reordered

explanation.surface: Dancers leaping in time seem to know each other's moves by instinct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in dance' rearranges THEY LEAP into TELEPAHY; T goes in after TELEPA.
explanation.definitionFit: Communicating mind to mind is often called a sixth sense beyond the usual five.

clue.text: Told Porky to have some rest

parts.note: porky is short for porky pie, Cockney rhyming slang for lie, so told a porky means lied
to own is to have or possess

explanation.surface: Someone told Porky the pig to take a break.
explanation.walkthrough: Porky pie is British rhyming slang for a lie, so 'Told Porky' (a porky) is LIED, not speech to a pig.
explanation.definitionFit: A lie-down is a short spell of resting on a bed or sofa, a bit of repose.

clue.text: Man almost catches delayed plane

indicators.note: catches means holds inside, so the word for delayed goes in
almost means not quite all, so the name loses its final letter

parts.note: Paul is a man's name
late means delayed

explanation.surface: A traveller only just makes a flight that was running late.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plane' is not an aircraft but a flat surface. 'almost' trims PAUL to PAU, which catches LATE.
explanation.definitionFit: A plateau is a raised stretch of flat land, and plane can mean a level, flat surface.

clue.text: What propels boat south — men at oar

parts.note: a rowing crew is the team pulling the oars

explanation.surface: A boat heads south with oarsmen rowing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'men at oar' sounds like the propulsion itself, but they give CREW; the propeller is the whole answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A ship's propeller is commonly called its screw, the rotating blades that drive it.

clue.text: Terrifying sound rocks Switzerland

parts.note: scree is loose broken rock on a mountainside
CH is the international vehicle code for Switzerland, from Confoederatio Helvetica

explanation.surface: A frightening noise shakes Switzerland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rocks' looks like a verb meaning shakes; it is a noun giving SCREE.
explanation.definitionFit: A screech is a harsh, piercing cry, the kind of noise that frightens.

clue.text: Vase for standing contains nothing in high place

indicators.note: contains means holds inside, so the letter for nothing goes within
in a down entry standing means set upright, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: a pot is a vessel such as a vase
taken as written
O looks like a zero, so it stands for nothing

explanation.surface: An upright vase is empty, sitting on a high shelf.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down light 'standing' means read upward, so the vase and 'for' come out backwards as ROFTOP before the zero-shaped O goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: The top of a building's roof is a lofty spot, an elevated position above the street.

clue.text: Expect payment where hospital refused to perform surgery

indicators.note: hospital refused means the hospital letter is turned away and removed

parts.note: to hope is to expect or look forward to
a rate is a charge or payment

explanation.surface: Someone expects to be paid when the hospital won't let them do the procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perform surgery' fits the hospital picture; the hospital is only the H dropped from HOPE RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: Surgeons are said to operate when they carry out a surgical procedure.

clue.text: Mares would triumph here, in sleep so monstrous

indicators.note: in means the answer lies within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Female horses win races in one's dreams, in a nightmare of a sleep.
explanation.walkthrough: Epsom Downs, Surrey, is a racecourse where the Oaks is run for fillies; the joke is that mares would win a race there.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsom Downs in Surrey is a famous racecourse, home of the Derby and the Oaks, where horses win races.

clue.text: Nobleman given honour as something of a listener

parts.note: an earl is a British noble
the OBE (Order of the British Empire) is a British honour

explanation.surface: A peer receives a royal decoration as a reward for being a good listener.
explanation.walkthrough: 'listener' is a person in the surface, but here it is an ear, and the answer is part of one.
explanation.definitionFit: A lobe is the soft lower part of the ear, the organ that does the listening.

clue.text: Demonstrators in rain?

definitions.meaning: people who show or display something

explanation.surface: Protesters marching through a downpour.
explanation.walkthrough: Demonstrators reads as protesters, but here it means people who display things, show-ers.
explanation.definitionFit: Short bursts of rainfall are called showers; and those who exhibit things are, playfully, show-ers.

clue.text: Thomas for one infected, cold caught

indicators.note: caught means trapped inside, so the cold letter goes within

parts.note: a septic wound is infected

explanation.surface: A patient with an infection has also caught a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thomas' is Doubting Thomas, the apostle who would not believe in the Resurrection until he saw it.
explanation.definitionFit: The apostle Thomas doubted until shown proof, making him the classic example of a doubter.

clue.text: Potter's work in poem has pun that's awful

indicators.note: something awful is a mess, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A poem with a dreadful pun in it, from a potter's craft.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potter' is not a pottery maker but Stephen Potter, whose 1952 book was titled 'One-Upmanship'. 'that's awful' rearranges IN POEM HAS PUN.
explanation.definitionFit: Stephen Potter wrote the humorous book of that title on gaining the advantage over others.
